therefore not ahistorical or abstract but historical and speciﬁc. is principle
of the speciﬁcity of divine revelation characterizes the past-historical
meaning of the text and makes evaluation necessary.
eologically speaking, this historical dimension of the revelation of G od
in the Bible relates to the doctrine of incarnation. A ccording to the Bible,
not only has the revelation of G od, that is, the W ord of G od, been
incarnated in the ﬂesh of Jesus; it has also been incarnated in historical acts
and human speech. is principle of accommodation is divine adaptation to
the human-historical situation. Christians tend to believe that their religion
is superior to other religions in part because of its historical and
incarnational nature, but this kind of revelation carries with it challenges of
its own.
First comes the situational challenge. History and human speech are by
nature situational. A t times human speech can transcend the situation in
which it was spoken, but it can never be entirely divorced from the situation.
W hen one comes to the Scriptures, one ﬁnds a kind of continuum  of
transcendence. Certain statements of Scripture directly express more
fundamental teachings, those that are less tied to the original situation into
which they were spoken, than do others (see ﬁg. 28).[26]
FIG U RE 28 
Continuum of transcendence
M ost biblical passages stand somewhere between the two extremes on the
continuum of transcendence, oen because some aspects of their teaching

--- Page 324 ---
are essentially transcendent while others are circumstantially contingent.
M oreover, even the statements that belong on the transcendent end of the
continuum are connected to some extent to the situation in which they were
originally articulated. No statement can be entirely divorced from its
original historical setting.[27]
A n example of a statement that seems to directly express more
fundamental teachings and to have only loose ties to the original situation is
G alatians 6:10: “W henever we have opportunity, let us work for the good of
all, and especially for those of the family of faith.” A n example of a statement
that seems to be closely tied to the original situation is 1 Timothy 5:23: “No
longer drink only water, but take a little wine for the sake of your stomach
and your frequent ailments.” Here the passage itself connects this instruction
to the physical condition that Timothy was experiencing at the particular
time, and no other passage in the biblical canon forbids the exclusive use of
water or demands the consumption of wine. Yet situation-bound statements
do not necessarily stand outside the possibility of contemporary
appropriation, since they are oen directly applicable today to essentially the
same situations or parallel ones.[28]
Obviously readers could not take over and directly apply some passages
no matter how much they might try to do so. us Deuteronomy 23:7 (“You
shall not abhor any of the Edomites, for they are your kin”) gives instruction
regarding relationships to a people who no longer exist. e point is clear:
One cannot simply assume that the surface meaning of any statement found
in the Scriptures can be directly appropriated in today’s contemporary
setting.
A t the same time, such a conclusion does not mean that passages one
judges to be circumstantially contingent have no applicatory potential.
A lthough usually one cannot legitimately appropriate the surface meaning
of passages that are circumstantially contingent, one oen ﬁnds that even
these passages have underlying teachings that one can reasonably and
legitimately appropriate. In such cases, one may not be able to appropriate
the answers to the deﬁnitive question from one’s interpretation, for the
answers to the deﬁnitive questions tend to deal with the surface meaning of
the text. But one may appropriate one’s answers to the rational and
implicational questions. e rational question probes the underlying
reasons, or rationale, for the statement, and quite oen at least some of these

--- Page 325 ---
reasons that stand behind a circumstantially contingent statement are
transcendent.[29] A nswering the implicational question divulges the
presuppositions and logical outgrowths of biblical passages. G enerally the
implications of a circumstantially contingent statement transcend the
original situation. e identiﬁcation of these underlying teachings in
circumstantially contingent passages is what W illiam J. W ebb calls moving
up the “ladder of abstraction.”[30]
A  second challenge that arises from the historical and incarnational
character of biblical revelation is the progress of revelation. e Bible-as-a-
whole, particularly as it culminates in the New Testament, clearly indicates a
progressive movement from the more primitive and incomplete revelation
in the earlier periods toward the more complete revelation in the later
periods, especially in Christ and his apostles. e Bible is not a ﬂat book but
a dynamic account of the revelation of G od throughout a long history.
e progress of revelation involves two elements. For one, a development
of revelation exists within the Old Testament-as-a-whole. A lthough this
development is certainly historical, involving the constant readaptation of
earlier biblical traditions by later Old Testament writers, one cannot assume
the ability to trace this revelatory development in the Old Testament simply
by tracking the theological and ethical ideas in the successive historical
stages of the production of the Old Testament.[31] e major problem here
is that even scholars cannot identify with assurance the speciﬁc historical
development of traditions in the Old Testament. Scholars represent a wide
divergence of thought about the dating of many Old Testament books. e
result is that in several cases one cannot speak conﬁdently about where a
given Old Testament witness falls within the historical sequence.[32]
Further, some Old Testament books give evidence of a more or less extended
history of the development of traditions within them, so that vestiges of
earlier theological and ethical ideas may stand alongside later ones in the
same book.[33] M oreover, the dynamics of the entire canon, especially in its
culmination in the New Testament, indicate that the progress of revelation
in the Old Testament is not ultimately a matter of historical sequence but of
theological and ethical proximity to G od’s ﬁnal revelation in Jesus Christ
and the New Testament.
us most Christians have good reason to think that the revelation of
G od is less complete or developed in the accounts of the wars of

--- Page 326 ---
extermination in Joshua, for example, than in the prophecies of G od’s
gracious forgiveness of Judah in the book of Jeremiah. at assessment
emerges ﬁnally not on the basis of historical sequence but out of an
acknowledgment that the revelation of G od’s superabounding forgiveness in
Jeremiah appears to be closer to the revelation of G od in Jesus Christ than is
the case with the wars of extermination in which G od destroyed not only the
leaders of the Canaanites but also voiceless women and children.[34]
A ll the same, to claim that some passages may contain relatively
incomplete or imperfect revelation is not to suggest that these passages have
no genuine revelatory signiﬁcance. To say that the revelation of G od is not
as complete in the wars of extermination as in certain other portions of the
Old Testament, such as the book of Jeremiah, is not to say that the wars of
extermination contain no true revelation of G od. e revelation of G od may
be less developed in the wars of extermination but is nevertheless real
revelation; indeed, some aspects of G od’s character and purpose may be
presented uniquely through the wars of extermination, so that one’s
understanding of G od would be deﬁcient if these accounts were absent from
the canon. Still, such passages do not oﬀer the ﬁnal word regarding G od’s
character and purpose, and any attempt to appropriate them must include a
serious process of evaluation that identiﬁes the situation-bound aspects that
would be illegitimate for persons today, in light of the principle of the
progress of revelation.
Yet the progress of revelation does not pertain only to development
within the Old Testament. e second element involved in the progress of
revelation is the relationship between the Old and New Testaments. is
relationship has been a diﬃcult problem since the beginning of Christianity.
It is perhaps accurate to say that the overarching theological problem in the
writings of the New Testament is the relationship between the covenants.
One might even go so far as to say that this focus remains the fundamental
issue in biblical theology and ethics and that almost every theological or
ethical issue is related more or less directly to it. One’s understanding of the
relationship between the Testaments will make a diﬀerence in terms of one’s
evaluation and appropriation of biblical statements.
roughout its history the church has clearly struggled with this issue of
the relationship between the Testaments; consequently, we would be foolish
to insist that our view be adopted as the correct one. Every student has the

--- Page 327 ---
responsibility to examine the biblical evidence inductively and on that basis
to determine what seems to be the most plausible understanding of this
relationship. It may be appropriate, however, for us to indicate one major
possibility and to describe, in general terms, how that understanding of the
relationship between the Testaments bears upon biblical evaluation.
W e ﬁnd that an examination of the Scriptures-as-a-whole indicates that
the Old Testament relates to the New Testament in terms of preparation and
fulﬁllment. e Old Testament prepares for the New Testament, and the
New Testament fulﬁlls the Old. Speciﬁcally, the two Testaments have a
dialectical relationship between them because the notion of preparation-
fulﬁllment involves essential continuity but with some discontinuity. Essential
continuity exists because the concept of fulﬁllment implies a profound and
fundamental connection with what preceded the fulﬁllment. But some
discontinuity exists since the concept of fulﬁllment implies also that
something has been added; it is not simply a continuation of what came
before. W e ﬁnd an element of culminative, or climactic, disjuncture. In
practice, altogether the New Testament sometimes conﬁrms (e.g., 1 Pet.
1:16; James 4:6; A cts 17:24–25), sometimes corrects (e.g., Heb. 4:8; M ark
10:4–5; G al. 5:6), sometimes expands the meaning of (e.g., M att. 2:15; 5:21–
30; A cts 2:25–28), and sometimes abrogates statements in the Old Testament
(e.g., M att. 5:38–45; M ark 7:14–23; A cts 10:1–48). e practical result is that
one must allow the New Testament to determine what continues to be of
value for direct appropriation in the Old Testament.[35]
e New Testament writers consistently aﬃrm, both explicitly and
implicitly, that the Old Testament is their authoritative Scripture. Indeed,
they seem to consider that discontinuities between Old Testament and New
Testament teaching actually arise out of a deeper and more profound
understanding of the Old Testament revelation of G od, and that this more
profound understanding is made possible by the eschatological fulﬁllment to
which the New Testament bears witness.
M oreover, the New Testament writers’ aﬃrmation of the continuing
authority of the Old Testament Scriptures suggests both that they generally
assume the ongoing validity of Old Testament teaching and that they wish
their audience to accept the teaching of the Old Testament as authoritative
except in the instances in which they indicate a modiﬁcation to the teaching
of the Old Testament. In the absence of such indicators, then, readers of the

--- Page 328 ---
New Testament should typically assume the continuing relevance of Old
Testament teaching.
A n example of this assumption of continuing relevance would be creation
theology. W ith the exception of claims about Christ’s role in creation and the
new creation, the New Testament says relatively little about creation,
compared to the much fuller treatment creation theology receives in the Old
Testament. In the view of some scholars,[36] Protestants especially have at
times focused so exclusively upon the New Testament that they have
practically neglected whole areas of biblical theology and ethics that pertain
to creation. Such neglect may in part lie behind the charge that Christians
have all too oen been neglectful of their stewardship of the environment.
NATU RE OF BIBLICAL ETHICS
us far we have seen that the necessity for evaluative biblical analysis
arises from the twofold nature of the Bible: it contains both past-historical
meanings of passages and their present-historical signiﬁcance, which
emerges from the speciﬁc past-historical meaning. But the necessity for
evaluative biblical analysis stems also from the nature of biblical ethics,
which is occasional rather than systematic. e Bible contains neither a
systematic theology nor a systematic code of ethics. Both the theological
assertions and the ethical instructions of the Bible were occasioned by the
situational demands that the biblical writers felt needed to be addressed.
us in terms of ethics, the Bible is not a lawbook but a collection of
occasional instructions. erefore students must evaluate each biblical
statement in terms of its role within the dynamic program of the
presentation of good and bad, right and wrong, true and untrue in the Bible-
as-a-whole.
To speak of a dynamic program of ethics within the Bible is to suggest the
existence of a profound and implicit structure to the ethics of the Bible.
Indeed, some sense of structure and of overarching dynamic connectedness
between biblical ethical statements is necessary in order to talk at all about
biblical ethics in the large. A n inductive examination of the ethics of the
Bible may reveal no overall structure to biblical ethics and that the various
ethical instructions throughout the Scriptures involve essentially isolated,
unrelated, and even contradictory moral counsel. But students are obliged to

--- Page 329 ---
explore whether in fact the Bible has within it a structure of ethics, and if so,
to identify the precise nature of this dynamic interconnectedness.
A lmost all scholars who discuss biblical ethics either explicitly or
implicitly adopt a structure of ethics that serves as the basis for their
discussions.[37] Yet in spite of the fact that the various presentations of the
structure of biblical ethics tend to have certain recurring emphases, at
present the precise shape of this structure has no consensus. erefore we
would be highly presumptuous to insist that our understanding of this
ethical structure is the only correct and proper one. Nevertheless, it may be
helpful to indicate one possible way of understanding the overarching shape
of biblical ethics and in the process to note certain features that scholars
repeatedly mention in their discussion of biblical ethics in the large. e
framework of biblical ethics depicted in ﬁgure 29 is based on our
interpretation of numerous biblical passages and our reading of the Bible-as-
a-whole. A s such it is admittedly tentative, and we do not mean to present it
as in any way deﬁnitive or ﬁnal. W e hope that it will at least be suggestive
and illuminating. W e will make no attempt to engage in the exhaustive task
of supporting this framework or its major components by argument or
extensive scriptural citation. Students who are familiar with the content of
the Bible will be able to recall biblical evidence for this model and its major
components.
A s we mentioned previously, the purpose of the Bible may be to bear
witness to the revelation of G od and of G od’s relationship with his,
especially human, creation; therefore the primary concern of the Bible is not
ethical but theological, so ethics derives from the primary theological focus
of the Bible. A s such, any adequate understanding of the ethical structure of
the Bible must emerge from the Bible’s theological emphases.
W e believe that the central theological concept in the Bible is the lordship
of G od;[38] the central aﬃrmation is that G od is actively at work to establish
his lordship over the cosmos, and especially over his human creation.
erefore the center of biblical ethics, the human moral obligation, is to
respond to G od’s lordship. is response involves the submission of selves to
the dynamic and redemptive lordship of G od. Every biblical instruction can
perhaps be traced back to this ultimate expectation.

--- Page 330 ---
FIG U RE 29 
Structure of biblical ethics
e reference to the submission of selves is intentional. A s we will
mention later, we do not intend that this emphasis upon selves should
diminish the vital role of community in ethics. Rather, by such an emphasis,
we attempt to acknowledge the Bible’s insistence that submission to the
lordship of G od involves a personal existential challenge to reject the claims
that the self places upon persons, and especially the claim that persons have
an ultimate obligation to the self (e.g., G en. 3:1–7; M ark 8:34) rather than to
G od or to others (e.g., M att. 22:15–22; Phil. 2:3–4; James 4:5–7).
M oreover, the Bible indicates that this submission of selves to the
redemptive lordship of G od is manifested in terms of relationships to the
three major realities that confront all humans: G od, others, and the
world/creation.[39] Since from the biblical viewpoint G od is the ultimate
reality in the universe, including the universe of human lives, the primary
relationship is with the Divine. A ccording to the Bible, humans are to relate
to G od in terms of what is true to G od. Because G od is the transcendent

--- Page 331 ---
creator, sustainer, and deliverer, humans are to worship him. Because G od is
faithful or trustworthy, humans are to respond accordingly by placing their
faith or conﬁdence in G od. Because G od is gracious, providing good and
withholding evil in ways that go far beyond what humans deserve, humans
are to be grateful and oﬀer thanks to G od. Because G od is demanding in his
loving expectations and consequently renders judgment upon those who
refuse to submit to his redemptive program, humans ought properly to fear
him. A nd because G od is love, humans can and should love him. Readers
who are familiar with the biblical text will immediately recall scriptural
passages that present these descriptions of G od and these expectations of
human response.
From the biblical viewpoint, this relationship with G od is a ﬁrst-order
relationship that leads inexorably to a second-order relationship with others
(e.g., M ark 12:28–31). Indeed, one’s relationship with G od inevitably
expresses itself in relationship with others (e.g., M att. 25:31–46; James 3:9; 1
John 4:16–21). A ccording to the Bible, humans are to relate to others in
terms of what is good for them, which is really love; for biblical love is “active
well wishing,” as James M oﬀatt describes it.[40] us many have argued that
love is the center of biblical ethics.[41] However, a more accurate depiction
says that love is the center, indeed the wellspring, of the ethics of human
interpersonal relationships (M att. 22:34–40). e G reek word the New
Testament typically employs for love is agape, so the model refers to ethical
obligation toward others as an agapocentric ethic.
But the Bible attends also to humans’ relationship to and responsibility
toward the created order. A ccording to the Bible, humans are to relate to
creation as agents of G od’s good rule over creation and thus do what is G od’s
will for it. Humans are, in a sense, G od’s vice-regents over creation (e.g.,
G en. 1:26–30), called not to plunder creation but to care for it (e.g., 2:15).
[42]
W ith regard to this model of biblical ethics, several emphases are worth
noting. First, this is a transcendent model in that it acknowledges the
initiation of G od as the basis for both the possibility and obligation of ethics.
Biblical ethics is, above all else, a response to what G od is and what G od has
done (e.g., Exod. 20:2; 1 John 4:19). e model emphasizes transcendence
also by acknowledging the role of the Son, through whom G od expresses his
lordship and through whom G od brings his lordship to realization. G od

--- Page 332 ---
expresses his rule through the Son personally as the Son embodies G od’s
kingdom. G od also expresses his lordship through the Son instrumentally
since the Son mediates the saving rule of G od to others. A nd the model
emphasizes transcendence in that it recognizes the role of the Spirit, who
makes operational the lordship of G od in the lives of individuals,
communities, and ultimately the world.
Second, this is a communal model: it acknowledges that G od intends to
begin the process of manifesting his lordship in the world through his
people, the community of faith. G od called Israel, and now calls the church,
to be the sphere where his lordship is particularly manifested through
worship toward G od, love among believers, and witness and service to the
world.
ird, this is a content-speciﬁc model in that it allows for each of the
categories herein described to be developed in terms of its presentation
within particular passages throughout the Bible.[43] Students must make a
vitally important decision not to treat these categories as broad abstractions
whose content is provided by one’s assumptions and personal predilections
rather than by the data of the biblical passages, properly interpreted.
Fourth, this is a developmental model: it recognizes that the actions of
G od in establishing his redemptive lordship and the consequent ethical
response on the part of humans are played out in a continuing historical
process that begins with creation and culminates with the new creation. e
Bible describes this progression from creation to new creation through the
salvation-historical meganarrative that moves from the ﬁrst covenant to the
new covenant, with Jesus Christ at the center. e notion of historical
progression is central, then, to one’s understanding of biblical ethics. A nd
the consideration of one’s own historical situation is critical for one’s
deliberations regarding the appropriation of the biblical ethic.
Finally, this is a holistic model: it recognizes that biblical ethics include
not merely behavior but also cognitive knowledge and transformed
character. One can fulﬁll the biblical expectations only if one knows what
those expectations are and what is involved in them; hence we refer to the
intellectual means of a mind informed by revelation. But the intellectual
means, though necessary, is not suﬃcient. e Bible is concerned not only
with overt behavior but also with one’s internal attitude and motive, in other
words, with matters of character; hence we refer also to the existential

--- Page 333 ---
means: to character, including emotions and will, transformed by the Holy
Spirit.
TYPES OF EVID ENCE FOR BIBLICAL ANALYSIS
e discussion of the necessity and nature of speciﬁc evaluation has
already introduced a number of principles that students should keep in
mind as they engage in speciﬁc evaluation. A t this point, however, focusing
on the process of assessing the legitimacy, scope, degree of force, and degree
of concession of biblical statements for contemporary appropriation is
appropriate. A n inductive approach requires that such assessment be made
on the basis of the careful consideration of evidence.[44]
Four types of scriptural evidence may be relevant in evaluating a biblical
statement. W e described most of these while treating interpretation in part 3
above; here we wish to highlight their signiﬁcance for evaluation. e
examples will reveal that in many cases the line between interpretation and
evaluation is diﬃcult to draw. Oen students will employ insights from the
interpretation and use them for the evaluation of a passage. e examples
will also demonstrate that in practice the various types of evidence have
signiﬁcant overlap; therefore, frequently two or more types of evidence may
be used in tandem. Finally, the examples will show that evaluation pertains
not only to the legitimacy of appropriating scriptural teachings in other
times and places, but also to the degree of concession, the degree of force,
and the scope of applicability.
Context. A s in interpretation, so also in evaluation, context is generally
the most signiﬁcant type of evidence; for context involves authorial
direction to the reader. Students should remember that context includes all
evidence within the biblical book.[45]
A ccording to M atthew 10:5–6, Jesus sent his disciples out on their
missionary journey, charging them to “go nowhere among the G entiles, and
enter no town of the Samaritans, but go rather to the lost sheep of the house
of Israel.” In M atthew’s G ospel the experience of the twelve disciples
typically anticipates that of the post-Easter church. erefore this passage
raises the question in the reader’s mind whether the instruction to limit
ministry to Israel pertained only to this moment in the Jesus-history, or
whether readers should take it up and directly appropriate it in other times

--- Page 334 ---
and places. e broad context of M atthew’s G ospel provides the answer. e
G ospel reaches its climax in the missionary commission of 28:18–20, where
the exalted Christ commands the post-Easter church to “make disciples of
all nations.” e broader context of the book, then, renders the statement in
10:5–6 situation-bound. It indicates that such restriction was appropriate for
the twelve disciples during Jesus’s earthly ministry, but that one cannot
legitimately and directly apply it during the period of the post-Easter
church. One’s earlier work in the interpretation of the passage may have
identiﬁed underlying reasons and theological implications that are
transcendent; thus these underlying reasons and theological implications
could serve as the basis for contemporary appropriation. But the surface
meaning of the passage is not directly applicable today.
Paul’s teaching regarding homosexual behavior in Romans 1:18–27 has
recently become a storm center of controversy, and this controversy pertains
especially to the signiﬁcance of immediate context for its evaluation. On the
basis of immediate context as well as historical background, some scholars
argue that Paul’s statements relate only to the connection between
homosexuality and idolatry as it was practiced in the ﬁrst century. ey
insist that Paul is attacking pagan idolatry and not homosexual practice as
such.[46] But we believe that a careful analysis of Paul’s argument reveals
that Paul grounds his objections to homosexual practice in the structure of
creation and that Paul insists that homosexual behavior represents human
resistance to the Creator. If so, immediate context suggests that Paul’s
teaching is transcendent and remains in force as long as creation stands.[47]
Contextual considerations are clearly relevant for the evaluation of Paul’s
statement, “I wish that all were [single] as I myself am” (1 Cor. 7:7; cf. 7:40).
e immediate context indicates that Paul views singleness as an ideal but
concedes that given the presence of strong sexual desires, most persons will
be unable to realize that ideal without the danger of falling into promiscuity
(7:2, 6, 8–9); only certain persons are gied by G od to remain single without
succumbing to the ﬂame of passion (7:8–9). Paul later bases this counsel on
the advisability that with the near arrival of the parousia, persons should
remain as free as possible from spousal responsibilities so as to direct all
their attention to the urgent work of G od (7:21–35). erefore these
contextual considerations indicate that (1) Paul presents this counsel as a
tactical suggestion: advice regarding what is most helpful under certain

--- Page 335 ---
circumstances over against an absolute command (degree of force); (2)
singleness is an ideal that allows for concession to human sexual realities
(degree of concession); and (3) this counsel is limited to those who are gied
by G od to live the single life without succumbing to sexual passions (scope
of applicability).
Scriptural testimony. e fact that the Bible is a canonical collection
suggests that students are responsible to answer the question of continuing
appropriation of individual biblical passages on the basis of the Bible-as-a-
whole. ose who embrace the notion of biblical authority should
understand that such authority does not ultimately belong to individual
passages read in isolation from the rest of the Bible; rather, biblical authority
involves the authority of the entire Bible. is authority implies the
importance of evaluating individual passages in light of their function
within the entire canon. us, in the process of evaluation, students should
always consider evidence from scriptural testimony, which includes all
evidence in the Bible outside of the biblical book itself.[48]
On the basis of contextual considerations, Paul’s instructions regarding
submission to governmental authorities in Romans 13:1–7 seems to be
unqualiﬁed: “ere is no authority except from G od, and those authorities
that exist have been instituted by G od,” with the result that “whoever resists
authority resists what G od has appointed, and those who resist will incur
judgment” because the authorities are “G od’s servant for your good, . . . the
servant of G od to execute wrath on the wrongdoer.” e fact that other New
Testament passages urge the same kind of submission (e.g., 1 Pet. 2:13–17) is
evidence from scriptural testimony that such submission is a transcendent
teaching. But additional evidence from scriptural testimony seems to
present an alternative perspective. us the book of Revelation portrays the
governing authorities as evil persecutors trying to force the faithful disciples
to abandon commitment to their Lord, and they should thus be resisted
even unto death (6:9–11; 9:1–11; 13:1–18:24). A nd A cts 3–5 presents the
Sadducean oﬃcials as religious leaders who yet function essentially as
political authorities, persecuting and trying to silence the apostles. e
apostles disregard the authorities’ demands and declare that it is better to
obey G od than humans (4:19; 5:29). M oreover, during his passion, Jesus
refuses to submit to the demands of Herod (Luke 23:6–12). erefore
scriptural testimony seems to qualify the instructions of Romans 13:1–7. It

--- Page 336 ---
indicates that submission to governing authorities is limited to situations in
which these authorities actually function in the (rather ideal) way Paul
describes them in this passage.
M any would argue for a tension in the New Testament regarding the role
of women in the church. A lthough the speciﬁc interpretation of passages
such as 1 Corinthians 14:33–36 and 1 Timothy 2:11–15 is disputed,[49] one
could plausibly construe these passages as forbidding any woman ever to
have teaching authority within the church. But other passages in the New
Testament may provide evidence from scriptural testimony suggesting that
these passages are situation-bound. For one thing, the Pauline Epistles
indicate elsewhere that women exercised leadership roles in the Pauline
churches: Paul refers to Junia as “prominent among the apostles” (Rom.
16:7),[50] and Euodia and Syntyche were women who apparently led
signiﬁcant groups within the Philippian church (Phil. 4:2–3).[51]
M oreover, the book of A cts reports that Priscilla, along with her husband,
A quila, took A pollos aside “and explained the W ay of G od to him more
accurately” (18:24–28).[52] A nd earlier the book of A cts records that
women were among the 120 in the upper room on the Day of Pentecost.
Everyone present in the upper room experienced the coming of the Spirit
and declared “the mighty works of G od” to all the people who were
assembled in Jerusalem (2:1–21 RSV; cf. 1:12–14), which Peter describes as
the fulﬁllment of Joel 2:28–32: “In the last days it will be, G od declares, that I
will pour out my Spirit upon all ﬂesh, and your sons and your daughters
shall prophesy. . . . Even upon my slaves, both men and women, in those
days I will pour out my Spirit; and they shall prophesy” (A cts 2:17–18). is
scriptural testimony may indicate that Paul’s instructions in 1 Corinthians
14:33–36 and 1 Timothy 2:11–15 had to do with speciﬁc situations current
at that time in the Corinthian and Ephesian churches.
A  ﬁnal example of scriptural testimony relates to the issue of slavery in
the Bible. U ndeniably, the Bible does not insist on abolition, and indeed
both the Old and New Testaments not only condone slavery but at points
may indicate that slavery is an appropriate part of the structuring of society
(e.g., Exod. 21:20–21, 28–32; Lev. 19:20–22; Deut. 23:15; Eph. 6:5–8; 1 Pet.
2:18–25).[53] Still, at least to most modern persons, slavery is a
contradiction of the command to love the neighbor as oneself, which Jesus
declares stands at the center of G od’s will as expressed in the law (M att.

--- Page 337 ---
22:34–40; cf. Lev. 19:18).[54] In these circumstances, then, the importance
of relating individual statements to the structure of biblical ethics becomes
apparent. If one evaluates slavery by the central command to love the
neighbor, one will conclude that the biblical ethics of interpersonal
relationships disallows the possibility of slavery and forces one to consider
any biblical statement that condones slavery to be situation-bound. e
biblical writers, in spite of their inspiration and genius, may have been so
enmeshed in a culture that assumed the role of slavery within society that
they were unable to conceive of a societal structure that did not include
slavery. W. J. W ebb refers to this kind of understandable cultural
enmeshment on the part of both biblical writers and audience as “limited
experiential horizon.”[55]
Scriptural testimony[56] raises the issue of competing texts in the Bible:
various biblical passages sometimes oﬀer diﬀerent, and perhaps even
seemingly contradictory, teaching. W e have seen that such a phenomenon
may point to one of the following possibilities: (1) it may indicate that
certain of these passages are actually addressing speciﬁc situations and are
thus situation-bound;[57] (2) it may point to the importance of situating
individual passages within the broad contours of the structure of biblical
ethics, so as to make a judgment between competing statements on the basis
of how these statements relate to the Bible’s central and primary concerns; or
(3) it may point to the progress of revelation between the Old Testament and
the New. W e now turn to this very issue.
Progress of revelation. e progress of revelation as evidence is actually a
subcategory of scriptural testimony. It pertains to the reality that we
described earlier, namely, that revelation within the Bible develops,
especially from the Old Testament to the New Testament; and it operates on
the basis of the principle that the New Testament adjudicates whether
certain statements in the Old Testament continue to have direct applicatory
validity
A  clear example of the progress of revelation is the list of antitheses in
M atthew 5:21–48. W e note especially the antithesis regarding lex talionis, or
the law of retaliation, in 5:38–42. Jesus quotes Exodus 21:24//Leviticus 24:20
verbatim, and in his “but I say to you” statement, Jesus contradicts the
surface meaning of the Old Testament instruction, “A n eye for an eye and a
tooth for a tooth.” Even if one grants that the purpose of the Old Testament

--- Page 338 ---
command was not to demand retaliation but to limit it,[58] one will
recognize that Jesus’s instruction requires a rejection of retaliation entirely.
e M atthean Jesus suggests that the command itself does not completely
express the will of G od that stands behind the letter; therefore Jesus fulﬁlls
the command through his antithetical demand (cf. 5:17–20). Jesus declares
this Old Testament command to be situation-bound, appropriate for the
people of Israel at the time M oses delivered the command to them but no
longer to be applied in the form in which it was given at that time. e
notion of the progress of revelation implies some divine accommodation to
the immaturity that naturally belonged to the earlier stages of the spiritual
development of G od’s people.[59]
A  second example of the progress of revelation emphasizes the element of
divine concession. In the passage dealing with the question of divorce (M ark
10:2–9), some Pharisees ask Jesus if a man may lawfully divorce his wife;
they remind Jesus that in the law “M oses allowed a man to write a letter of
dismissal and to divorce her.” But Jesus explains that the M osaic legislation
was a divine concession: “Because of your hardness of heart he wrote this
commandment to you. But from the beginning of creation, ‘G od made them
male and female.’ ‘For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother
and be joined to his wife, and the two shall become one ﬂesh.’ . . . erefore
what G od has joined together, let no one separate.” Here Jesus declares that
G od’s stated purposes in creation show that the divorce legislation did not
reﬂect the divine ideal but was rather a concession to human sinfulness; thus
the validity of the M osaic legislation was limited to the time when persons
experienced bondage to hardness of heart, from which they can now be
freed because of the arrival of the end-time kingdom of G od (cf. M ark 1:14–
15).
One may judge even certain elements in the creation account to be
situation-bound on the basis of progress of revelation. e command to
marry, or at least the expectation of marriage, which is found in G enesis
2:24, is challenged in the New Testament by both Jesus (M att. 19:10–12) and
Paul (1 Cor. 7:6–9, 21–38) in favor of the ideal of singleness for the sake of
the kingdom, at least for those who are gied by G od for the life of
singleness.[60]
H istorical and cultural background. A t times the historical or cultural
background of a biblical statement can inform one’s evaluation of its

--- Page 339 ---
contemporary applicatory value. One frequently articulated principle states
that if a given biblical statement stands in continuity with assumptions and
expectations of the surrounding culture (paracultural), the statement is
more likely, although by no means certain, to be cultural, that is, situation-
bound. Conversely, if a given biblical statement contradicts or challenges the
assumptions and expectations of the surrounding culture (countercultural),
it is more likely to be transcultural, that is, transcendent.[61] us, insofar as
the cultures that surrounded ancient Israel were polytheistic, the insistence
of the Old Testament on the exclusive worship of Yahweh is, in terms of
evidence from historical background, more likely to have transcendent
applicatory validity. In the same way, the fact that the cultures that
surrounded ancient Israel as well as the G reco-Roman world accepted or
perhaps even celebrated homosexual behavior[62] likely renders the biblical
prohibitions of such behavior transcendent. A dditionally, the fact that
polygamy was apparently generally accepted in the ancient Near Eastern
cultures that surrounded ancient Israel may support the conclusion that
such practice, as represented on the pages of the Old Testament, is situation-
bound.[63]
In addition, an examination of the cultural background of language
employed in biblical passages can assist students in identifying the culturally
embedded character of certain instructions. For example, such an
examination would be helpful for the assessment of Paul’s statements in 1
Corinthians 11:5–6, a passage that strikes most modern readers as odd and
puzzling: “A ny woman who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered
disgraces her head—it is one and the same thing as having her head shaved.
For if a woman will not veil herself, then she should cut oﬀ her hair; but if it
is disgraceful for a woman to have her hair cut oﬀ or to be shaved, she
should wear a veil.” K lein, Blomberg, and Hubbard nicely summarize the
signiﬁcance of cultural background for this passage:
ese remarks [from Paul] drive the reader to ask what was disgraceful about shaved heads
among women of Paul’s day. Numerous possibilities exist. For Jewish women shaved heads may
have suggested that they were guilty of adultery. For G reco-Roman women shaved heads may
have indicated that they were the more “masculine” partner in a lesbian relationship. So unless
short hair or uncovered heads send similar signals in modern-day cultures, . . . the speciﬁc
practice here is irrelevant. On the other hand, any dress or grooming, behavior or conversation
that suggests sexual unfaithfulness or deviance should remain as wrong for Christian women
today as it was in ﬁrst-century Corinth.[64]

--- Page 340 ---
us a recognition of the cultural background can reveal possibilities for
appropriation in passages that may initially appear to oﬀer little signiﬁcance
for contemporary audiences.
D ISTINCTIONS IN PROCESS BETW EEN OLD TESTAM ENT AND NEW
TESTAM ENT PASSAGES
A lthough the general procedure of evaluation is constant for all passages
throughout the Bible, some distinctions in process exist between the
assessment of Old Testament and New Testament passages. Old Testament
passages, aer all, represent an earlier stage in the progress of divine
revelation.
Old Testament passages should be evaluated in light of their place in the
Old Testament and in light of speciﬁc New Testament statements and overall
New Testament teachings. In Joel 2:12–17, for example, the prophet calls the
people of Judah to repentance; they sinned and were consequently physically
devastated by G od’s judgment. e prophet supports this call to repentance
with the promise that G od will then reverse the judgment of physical
distress and send them material blessings, agricultural plenty for those who
repent and submit in obedience to G od’s will (2:14). e following passage
assumes that Judah has accepted the prophet’s summons to repentance and
has turned from its sinful ways so as to submit in obedience to G od’s
righteous will. It describes the lavish physical blessing that Yahweh has
consequently bestowed upon the newly obedient Judah (2:18–27). e book
of Joel, then, oﬀers a clear causal connection: sin results in physical distress
and material deprivation, but repentance and renewed faithfulness to
Yahweh will result in physical, material bounty.
is view that sin will lead to physical and material judgment while
righteousness will lead to material blessing from Yahweh is conﬁrmed in
many other passages in the Old Testament. Indeed, the aﬃrmation that G od
will materially reward the righteous and bring material devastation upon the
unrighteous is a hallmark of the Deuteronomic theology, which according to
most scholars is found in many parts of the Old Testament (including, for
example, Jeremiah). It is expressed, among other places, in the contrasting
lists of blessings and curses in Deuteronomy 27–28 and the summarizing
conclusion in Deuteronomy 30. A  signiﬁcant portion of the Old Testament

--- Page 341 ---
wisdom tradition also insists on a causal connection between submitting to
the way of the Lord, which is the path of wisdom, and material prosperity
over against a corresponding causal connection between foolishness and
physical suﬀering/devastation. e book of Proverbs draws these
connections repeatedly.[65]
Yet this view is also challenged in the Old Testament. e wisdom
tradition engaged in its own critique of a simple and direct connection
between righteousness and material blessing on the one hand, and between
unrighteousness and material or physical devastation on the other. us the
book of Job describes a man who suﬀers not simply in spite of his
righteousness but also because of it, although in the end his faithfulness to
G od leads to his receiving double what he had at the beginning (Job 42:10–
17). M oreover, the Servant of the Lord in Isaiah 40–55 suﬀers physical pain,
hardship, and even death as a consequence of his utter righteousness. But
this view is generally quite foreign to the Old Testament, as even the
opening lines of Isaiah 53 attest: “W ho has believed what we have heard?
A nd to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?”
e New Testament does not promise that believers will have physical
blessing and prosperity because they are disciples of Christ, and certainly
faithful and obedient churches receive no such promise. Indeed, the New
Testament-as-a-whole teaches that physical adversity and sacriﬁce of wealth,
and even material deprivation, may accompany discipleship. Speciﬁc
examples include M atthew 5:10–12; 19:27–29; M ark 8:34–37; and Hebrews
10:33–34. But the ultimate example is the experience of Jesus himself:
though he was rich, he became poor (2 Cor. 8:9); unlike even the birds and
foxes, he had nowhere to lay his head (Luke 9:58). His obedience led him to
the way of the cross and suﬀering, to the loss of all the material blessings of
this life.
A s far as the New Testament is concerned, righteousness issues in
blessing. Yet the promised reward is not physical or material blessing in this
life but spiritual blessing now and eternal bliss in the world to come. e
book of Joel contains, then, a fundamental truth that is still relevant:
Righteousness produces blessing; obedience is the secret to well-being. e
teaching of Joel reaches its fulﬁllment in the New Testament; but precisely
because it is fulﬁllment, the New Testament teaching transcends the earlier
articulation in Joel and is thus diﬀerent in certain signiﬁcant ways. G od

--- Page 342 ---
revealed this truth to the generation of Joel in the only terms in which that
Old Testament generation could understand it, given where that generation
was in the centuries-long process of G od’s developing his people toward
fuller understanding and maturity.
From this discussion, students should not conclude that their personal
appropriation or their pastoral proclamation of the book of Joel must
remain at the level of the general notion that righteousness, or a return to
righteousness, produces blessing. If that were the case, the book of Joel
would not make its own unique contribution to biblical faith. It would tell
readers nothing more than what they could ﬁnd, expressed in much clearer
fashion, on the pages of the New Testament. But in fact the book of Joel
contains certain aspects of this fundamental truth that are not found in quite
the same way anywhere else in the biblical canon. In other words, the book
of Joel continues to bear its own witness to New Testament faith. One might
note, for example, how Joel emphasizes that G od is under no obligation to
reward those who return to a life of faithful obedience; rather, such a
decision to bless those who assume the mantle of righteousness is a matter
of grace: “W ho knows whether he will not turn and relent, and leave a
blessing behind him?” (2:14). e book of Joel also teaches that G od so
rejoices at the repentance of his people that he is inclined to favor those who
turn from wickedness to righteousness, to give them blessings that go far
beyond what they enjoyed in the past or could ever have expected to receive
(2:28–3:21).
A s for New Testament statements, they should be evaluated in light of
overall New Testament teachings and other speciﬁc New Testament
passages. In M ark 10:17–22, for example, we note Jesus’s injunction to the
rich young man. In response to the man’s question, “W hat must I do to
inherit eternal life?” Jesus responds, “G o, sell what you own, and give the
money to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow
me.” e issue may be put this way: Is this command a general requirement
for discipleship and eternal life? Can this statement be taken up and directly
applied in other times and other places, including our own? A lthough both
the immediate context (10:23–31) and several other New Testament
passages emphasize the danger of attachment to riches and the importance
of giving sacriﬁcially to the poor,[66] in the New Testament-as-a-whole such
action is not seen as generally necessary for discipleship. Speciﬁc passages

--- Page 343 ---
include the Zacchaeus story in Luke 19:1–10, in which Zacchaeus oﬀers to
repay fourfold anyone he has defrauded and to give half of his possessions to
the poor, but presumably he maintains a signiﬁcant portion of his
possessions. Joseph of A rimathea is described in M atthew 27:57 as a rich
man who was also a disciple of Jesus. e book of A cts describes M ary the
mother of John M ark as continuing to own a house (12:6–17), even in the
midst of a narrative reporting that “as many as owned lands or houses sold
them and brought the proceeds . . . [and] laid it at the apostles’ feet” (4:34–
35). Paul instructs Timothy regarding pastoral care toward the wealthy in
the church (1 Tim. 6:17–19).
e transcendent teaching of M ark 10:17–22, then, seems to be that one
must take every step necessary, even the most draconian, so as to remove
any hindrance that may stand in the way of discipleship to Christ. at is the
teaching of the passage, which applies to all persons in all times and places.
But the passage also suggests that although materialism is oen a chief issue
to be addressed as one considers becoming a disciple of Jesus, it was an issue
especially in the case of this particular man. erefore individuals should
examine their own set of commitments, whatever those may be, to
determine what kinds of decisions it might be necessary for each of them to
undertake in order to follow Christ. ey must boldly make these decisions,
no matter how costly the decisions are. e New Testament indicates that
certain persons may maintain a kind of sanctiﬁed distance toward their
possessions. In other words, certain persons are able to manage their
possessions while considering them as actually belonging to G od and given
by G od in trust for their use in G od’s kingdom, as did the mother of John
M ark in the book of A cts.
In Romans 14:1–15:13, Paul addresses the issue of an apparent
controversy within the Roman church regarding whether the Old Testament
calendrical observances (14:5–6) and especially dietary laws (14:2, 6, 14–23)
[67] continue to be required for Christians, or whether Christians are free
from such requirements. is controversy seems to have led to a spirit of
quarreling (14:1) and judgmentalism (14:3, 10, 13), which threatened the
unity of the Roman church (14:1, 19; 15:7), for such unity is made possible
only by a generous attitude toward those who diﬀer from us and a self-
sacriﬁcial spirit (14:1, 15, 20; 15:1–6). Paul insists that no theological basis
exists for the continuing observance of these calendrical and dietary

--- Page 344 ---
requirements, and he agrees that those who continue to observe them are in
a sense “weak” (14:1; 15:1). He urges that such weak Christians should
recognize that so long as those who eat and drink have a clear conscience
before the Lord, the weaker Christians should respect their decision (14:4–
12).
Nevertheless, Paul also insists that Christians who realize that they are
free to ignore these ordinances should observe them if their failure to
observe them causes a brother or sister to be spiritually injured (14:15) or
even to stumble away from the faith (14:21). Scriptural testimony indicates
that the teaching of this passage may be transcendent. Paul makes a similar
argument in 1 Corinthians 8:1–9:27 and 10:23–11:1, where he insists that
nothing in principle makes eating meat oﬀered to idols objectionable, yet
Christians ought to abandon such practice if it oﬀends other members of the
Christian community to the point that it may cause them to stumble away
from the faith. A nd the same balancing of Christian freedom from Old
Testament dietary regulations with concern for the scruples of others in the
community lies behind the delicately nuanced judgment of the church at the
apostolic council in A cts 15:1–41.
us the principle enunciated in Romans 14:1–15:13 is transcendent, but
the speciﬁc issue of the calendrical and dietary ordinances involves a certain
local problem in the Roman church at that time. is problem has little
relevance for most modern readers, not because it is inherently unimportant
but because of its obsolescence.[68] erefore the speciﬁc teaching is
situation-bound, and with few exceptions these particular circumstances no
longer obtain in the Christian church.[69] But the underlying principle,
which Paul makes explicit in the passage, can be taken up and applied in
other times and places: Christians have certain peripheral areas in their
experience in which their conscience alone should be the authority as to
whether or not a particular practice should be followed and in determining
what their decision should be. ey should be guided by three primary
considerations: their faith-relationship before G od, what is best for the
spiritual well-being of their fellow Christians, and the welcoming peace and
unity of the church.
SITU ATIONAL ANALYSIS

--- Page 345 ---
Not only does the biblical teaching require assessment; so does the
contemporary situation or issue to which we think the biblical teaching
might apply. e purpose of this assessment is to ascertain whether, and if
so, how, the contemporary situation relates to the biblical truth. is
necessity for situational analysis arises from three considerations.
First, even as biblical evaluation is necessary because of the historical
character of the Bible and revelation within the Bible, so also situational
analysis is necessary because persons’ own lives are profoundly historical:
they involve highly speciﬁc and historically conditioned situations. In order
to be true to the realities of appropriation, one must give attention not only
to the historically speciﬁc character of the originating revelation (biblical
analysis) but also to the historically speciﬁc character of the receptor
situation (situational analysis).
Second, the necessity of situational analysis arises from the consideration
that the ethics of the Bible are arguably principle-based rather than legal-
based. e possibility of the principle-based character of biblical ethics is
reﬂected above in ﬁgure 29 (“Structure of biblical ethics”). In it we suggest
that the Bible presents ethical obligation in terms of principles (e.g.,
thankfulness, love) rather than a legal code.[70] e function, or at least the
goal, of law is to attempt to incorporate every conceivable situation into the
legal code.[71] But a principle-based ethic requires that persons consider
carefully how they might relate the principle to their own situation with as
much integrity as possible. erefore students must take the biblical ethical
principles, speciﬁcally interpreted, and relate them thoughtfully to situations
in which students ﬁnd themselves in order to determine exactly how the
biblical principle can most properly be translated into particular situations.
W e do not mean that applying certain biblical commands directly would be
improper, but one would do so insofar as the command is a concretization
of the principle to a situation that parallels, or corresponds to, today’s
contemporary situation.[72]
e necessity of translating the biblical principles into readers’ particular
situations pertains to all the principles, or categories, described in the model
of the “Structure of biblical ethics” that we presented (ﬁg. 29). Take, for
example, the principle, or category, of worship. e Bible ﬁlls the principle of
worship with speciﬁc content, which one can derive from a careful study of
the various biblical passages that deal with worship. us certain constants

--- Page 346 ---
are present in every attempt to apply the biblical mandates for divine
worship. But all communities, and all individuals, must consider how to
translate the biblical vision and demands of worship into their speciﬁc
situations, allowing for some diﬀerences in the ways in which worship is
pursued, or conducted, from one community to another and even, in some
ways, from one person to another.
But the role of the contemporary situation is especially prominent with
the principle of love. A  love-centered (agapocentric) ethic requires that each
person, or each community, ask, W hat is the most loving thing to do in this
particular situation? But immediately one must qualify the phrase “most
loving thing” as what is the most loving action according to G od’s perspective
as set forth in the Scriptures. e problem with the situation ethics that
gained prominence in the 1960s and is especially associated with the
popular book by Joseph Fletcher, Situation Ethics: e New M orality,[73] is
not that it insisted on an agapocentric ethic in persons’ relationships with
others, for such is the biblical view. Instead, the problem is that love was
oen deﬁned as that which an individual considers to be the loving thing to
do in this or that situation. is understanding of love, then, tends to be
human-centered (anthropocentric) and individual-centered (idiocentric),
whereas the ethic of the Bible is G od-centered (theocentric) in terms of its
nature and character, and Christ-centered (christocentric) in terms of its
ultimate expression and manifestation.
e third necessity of situational analysis arises from the fact that
contemporary situations into which scriptural truth is appropriated are oen
highly complex; they therefore require careful analysis in order to
understand them with suﬃcient thoroughness and clarity to appropriate the
Bible to them in responsible ways. Sometimes, of course, situational analysis
is rather simple: a more or less straight line runs between the biblical
teaching and its application to our lives. But one should be careful to
recognize that certain contemporary situations appear simple and
straightforward and yet may turn out to be more complex than they
originally appear. W hen considering how to appropriate a biblical teaching
to any contemporary situation, one should always pause to consider whether
this contemporary situation involves more than meets the eye.
Some contemporary situations, however, are quite obviously complex.
Such would be the case with certain major ethical issues that occupy

--- Page 347 ---
attention in the modern world. James G ustafson has helpfully suggested four
steps in the analysis of complex situations.[74]
1. H istorical analysis. How does the history of a contemporary ethical
action/problem illumine it? For example, in the case of capital punishment,
how does an understanding of the history of capital punishment illumine
the issues involved in capital punishment? M ore speciﬁcally, one might ask,
W hat have been the use, eﬀects, and advantages and disadvantages of capital
punishment? In the case of animal cloning, how does the history of animal
cloning or related scientiﬁc ventures illumine the issues involved? (Since
animal cloning is a relatively recent phenomenon, the data here may be
limited but useful insofar as they exist.)
2. M otivational analysis. W hat are the motivations and intentions at work
in the various views on this ethical issue, such as capital punishment or
animal cloning?
3. Circum stantial analysis. W hat is now occurring as a result of a given
ethical action/problem? A re the motivations and intentions involved in a
given ethical action/problem being realized? In terms of speciﬁc examples,
what is occurring now as the result of current policy and practice (or
nonpractice) of capital punishment/animal cloning? A re the motivations
and intentions behind these policies/practices being realized in them?
4. Consequential analysis. W hat alternative courses of action might be
followed? W hat would be the (likely) consequences of these courses of
action? In terms of our examples: W hat would likely result from following
other practices than those currently in place? W ould those results more
eﬀectively fulﬁll the good motivations and intentions regarding capital
punishment/animal cloning?[75]
Clearly this kind of analysis requires one to consider extrabiblical
materials, especially from the sciences—both the physical sciences and the
social/behavioral sciences. For example, one would need to consult a history
of capital punishment to gain information necessary for historical analysis,
or one would need to consult studies of the physiology of cloned animals to
obtain information for circumstantial analysis. But one should remember
that almost no scientiﬁc research is entirely deﬁnitive, and none is
completely objective. Not only social/behavioral sciences (so sciences) but
also the physical sciences (hard sciences) are vulnerable to the bias of
researchers and scholars.[76] us, if possible, students should consult

--- Page 348 ---
studies produced by reputable scientists who represent a variety of points of
view; they should assess these studies critically on the basis of evidence and
valid conclusions from evidence.
But one should not assume that careful analysis is necessary only in
relation to major ethical issues that confront modern society. Such analysis
may be required for accurate and helpful appropriation of biblical teaching
to situations in one’s own individual life or in the lives of congregations.
ese individual or local situations can sometimes be quite complex; or at
least they might contain deeper issues that beg to be addressed in creative
and healing ways through the appropriation of biblical truth. A s G rant
Osborne writes: “e preacher must in a very real sense become a
sociologist analyzing the social and ethical needs of the ﬂock before
applying the text to meet those needs. In some ways it is as important to
analyze the congregation’s needs accurately as it is to exegete the text
correctly.”[77] ose who are engaged in teaching or preaching in the
church should take special care to analyze the needs or situations of those to
whom they minister so as to appropriate biblical teaching in a correct and
eﬀective manner.
Situational analysis may also have a bearing on decision making when
biblical norms seem to conﬂict. Norman G eisler points out that “evangelicals
have generally held to some form of ethical absolutism. In contrast to
situationalism, they have claimed that there are many moral absolutes.” He
adds, “W ithin the camp of those holding to two or more absolutes, a special
problem arises: W hat about moral conﬂicts? at is, what ought one to do
when two or more of his absolute obligations come to unavoidable conﬂict?”
In contrast to the options of “unqualiﬁed absolutism” and “conﬂicting
absolutism” as responses to this ethical dilemma, G eisler prefers “graded
absolutism (or the greater good position),” which holds “that real moral
conﬂicts do sometimes occur, but . . . that one is personally guiltless if he
does the greatest good in that situation.”[78]
Appropriation
A ppropriation involves the correlation of the biblical truth with the
contemporary situation in order that the biblical truth might profoundly

--- Page 349 ---
inform the contemporary situation. M uch that we have described in the
discussion of the dual processes of biblical and situational analysis
contributes to the work of appropriation. But now we brieﬂy discuss some of
the major aspects of appropriation proper.
e process of relating a biblical statement or teaching to a contemporary
situation requires a true correspondence between the two. erefore one
must determine that the biblical teaching does actually relate to a given
contemporary situation. Even transcendent teachings cannot be applied
indiscriminately to all situations.
erefore the possibility of appropriating the teaching of a biblical
passage to a contemporary situation requires a direct connection between the
teaching of the passage and the contemporary situation.[79] A ppropriating
even situation-bound teachings to contemporary situations is ﬁtting, but
only if the contemporary situation is indeed parallel with the circumstances
of the passage in which the situation-bound teaching occurs. us, if one’s
health were negatively aﬀected by the poor quality of available water and the
use of wine or medications containing alcohol would restore health without
adverse eﬀects, the situation-bound teaching of 1 Timothy 5:23 would be
directly applicable. But in the case of a person with a history of alcoholism,
such application would be ruinous and diametrically contrary to the
purpose of the passage.
If one wishes to appropriate the transcendent teachings of a passage,
either one must assess a speciﬁc contemporary situation to ascertain
whether it falls within the bounds of the transcendent teaching or one must
identify a contemporary situation that does. For example, if one is
considering appropriating the transcendent teachings of Romans 14:1–15:13
to a certain practice, one must ﬁrst ascertain whether that practice may be
validly considered peripheral or whether it is central and essential in nature.
If the practice is essential, the employment of Romans 14:1–15:13 may lead
to license rather than to true Christian freedom.
In this regard an excellent test is to compare the practice in question with
the concrete situation to which Paul addressed his words. A nything that is
fundamentally similar to the practice of eating or not eating meat in that
setting may be judged to be peripheral. In contrast, if a contemporary
practice is basically diﬀerent from eating meat as understood in that setting,
then it is essential rather than peripheral. us, if the characteristics of the

--- Page 350 ---
problem of eating meat are present in the contemporary situation, then the
contemporary situation ﬁts the situation of the passage in Romans. If,
however, they are basically diﬀerent, such as would be true if the
contemporary problem were one of idolatry or extramarital sexual relations,
then one could not legitimately apply Paul’s statements to it.
Students have two broad possibilities for relating the teaching of a biblical
passage to a contemporary situation. One possibility is to begin with the
study of a biblical passage; aer interpreting that passage, students might
choose to pursue its contemporary applicatory possibilities. A s we have just
mentioned, in such a case they would be careful to identify contemporary
situations that do relate directly to the biblical truth that is to be
appropriated.
But quite oen students come to the Bible with questions or issues they
are facing, either personally or in their communities, seeking to ﬁnd answers
or guidance from the text. e second possibility for relating biblical
teaching to a contemporary situation, then, is to ﬁnd biblical passages that
relate to the issue at hand and to interpret and evaluate them fairly and on
their own terms. In such a case a possible approach would be to employ a
reliable topical concordance[80] to identify passages throughout the Bible
that seem to bear on the issue; aer carefully reading each of these passages
in its context, students would locate the one passage that seems to be most
pertinent. If a single passage does not obviously stand out, students would
then locate the passages that seem to relate most directly to their
contemporary concern. A t this point, however, students must be careful that
they are basing the selection upon the principle of the degree of relatedness
and not on the basis of a desire to choose passages that appear to oﬀer
answers they expect or hope to ﬁnd.
A er they have identiﬁed the most pertinent passage(s), students should
engage in the process of observation, interpretation, and evaluation as the
basis for the appropriation of the passage to the issue at hand. Students
should always be alert to the possibility that the interpretation of a passage
that initially appeared to relate to their contemporary concern may reveal
that the passage does not deal speciﬁcally or helpfully with that concern at
all. In such a case, students would be forced to pursue help from other
passages that do in fact inform one’s contemporary situation. Students
should also be open to the possibility that the guidance a passage oﬀers for

--- Page 351 ---
their contemporary concern might be quite diﬀerent from what they
expected or wanted to ﬁnd. A n inductive commitment would require that
they follow the biblical teaching wherever it might lead.
In a sense, the appropriation of a passage represents the sum total of
biblical and situational analysis. W hen one has identiﬁed the biblical
teaching that has continuing applicatory validity as well the contemporary
situation to which the biblical teaching can properly be applied, then one
may bring the passage to bear on the situation, and the result is
appropriation.
e following is an illustration of the broad contours of this process from
Joel 2:12–17:
e sin of Judah resulted in physical distress and material deprivation,
while Judah’s repentance and renewed faithfulness to Yahweh result in
physical, material bounty.
Sin results in spiritual distress and eternal judgment, while repentance
and renewed faithfulness to G od result in spiritual blessings and eternal
reward.
You are sinners and have not repented and submitted to G od’s will; or
you are sinners and have repented and submitted to G od’s will.
erefore you should know that G od will judge you with spiritual
distress now and eternal condemnation in the world to come; or you
should embrace the reality that G od will reward you richly with
spiritual blessings now and with eternal life in the world to come.
Students will note that this illustration sets forth the basic process of
application. In practice, they would need to incorporate particular content
from the interpretation and evaluation of the passage so as to arrive at a
more speciﬁc and rich appropriation. is appropriation should be
materially speciﬁc and functionally broad.
A ppropriation should be materially speciﬁc in that the student should aim
at the greatest possible degree of particularity in appropriating the biblical
materials. Students should always ask, In what speciﬁc ways does this
appropriation of the biblical teaching to my contemporary situation inform
my thinking and behavior regarding this contemporary situation? Exactly
how will my thinking and behavior be diﬀerent than it was before I engaged

--- Page 352 ---
in this process of appropriation? W hat particular and concrete changes does
my appropriation of this biblical teaching require of me in this situation? It
is both an ineﬀective and a dangerous practice to remain at the level of
broad generalities in biblical appropriation. Since human lives are
characterized by particularity, such a practice will tend to make the work of
appropriation meaningless and irrelevant; or it will lead to implicitly
introducing more speciﬁc applicatory content that may have little to do with
the speciﬁc teaching of the biblical passage and indeed may contradict it.
However, appropriation should also be functionally broad, in terms of
both the process of appropriation and the range of application. e process of
appropriation should be broad in that it involves both individual and
communal aspects. In a sense every individual has the responsibility to
search the Scriptures for oneself in order to ﬁnd guidance and to experience
personal formation. But in another sense the believer experiences the
formational power of the Scriptures through participation in a community
of faith, which is at least potentially the community where the formation of
biblical values is communicated and nurtured.
Birch and Rasmussen describe the role of community well:
W e cannot and do not muster moral insight for ourselves by ourselves apart from our
communities, any more than we are or can be human beings apart from others. Everything we
know about morality and the moral life, or anything else, for that matter, is ﬁnally a community
enterprise and achievement. W hile it is true that individuals are not simply community clones,
are unique, and may well rise above the moral level of their communities, it is true with equal
force that even the most private decisions and achievements are the results of our social
experience and could neither exist nor be understood apart from that experience.[81]
ey go on to point out that for the moral life, the role of experiencing
Christian community is especially signiﬁcant: “In sum, both Judaism and
Christianity conceived of the moral life as the practical outcome of the
community’s faith, as shown in the sorts of lives members of the community,
and the community as a whole, lived. e community’s task was to socialize
its members into forms of life which displayed the kind of conduct beﬁtting
the experience of G od in community.”[82] A nd this moral socialization
comes about through the community’s common study and embodiment of
biblical truth.[83]
is emphasis on the role of Christian community for moral decision
making suggests that the church should be a forum for Christian moral

--- Page 353 ---
discourse, where discussions of the proper Christian response to major
ethical issues facing individuals, the church, and society at large are
conducted.[84] ese issues are oen so complicated that individuals ﬁnd
them impossible either to understand adequately or to make biblically
informed judgments about. M oreover, Christians have biblical warrant for
believing that G od intends for the church to be divinely gied to discern the
truth of the Scriptures and to translate that truth into moral decisions and
behavior.[85]
e structures of community life that are typically already in place oﬀer a
range of venues in which these issues can be explored from a biblical
perspective, including Bible study groups, Sunday school classes, seminars,
and forums. Such discussions need to be self-critical and methodologically
responsible, reﬂecting the kinds of principles and processes set forth here.
A lso, continuous open conversation between churches and denominations
on these issues is an all-important factor; otherwise, such group discussions
will serve only to intensify and validate community prejudices.
e role of the church in moral decision making includes also the
deliberations and judgments of the church throughout its history. Christians
can gain much insight into the process of ethical reﬂection and biblical
appropriation by drawing upon the cumulative wisdom of the church, in
which the Holy Spirit dwells. In hindsight, one can see that at certain points
in history some Christian communities have faltered in their attempts to
appropriate biblical truth to their contemporary settings, as for example in
the notorious arguments made to support the A frican slave trade. Yet in a
sense these errors are a gi to contemporary Christians who can learn from
the church’s mistakes in moral decision making as well as from its successes.
[86]
But appropriation should be functionally broad not only in terms of the
process of application, involving both the individual and the corporate, but
also in terms of the range of application. e Bible addresses the whole of life
in all of its aspects; and students’ appropriation of biblical teachings must be
equally broad. For one thing, biblical appropriation involves both thinking
and acting. e Bible is concerned not simply with overt actions but also
with the processes, direction, and content of thinking. Indeed, the Bible
recognizes that behavior typically stems from thinking. It recognizes the
power of what people today call belief systems. For that reason Paul

--- Page 354 ---
frequently structures his epistles by moving causally from the indicative of
doctrine, or beliefs, to the imperative of action (e.g., Rom. 12:1–2; Eph. 4:1–
2). A lthough seemingly strange and inadequate to the pragmatically
oriented modern W estern mind, an appropriation that is essentially
ideological is entirely valid. But the example from Paul’s Epistles reminds
students also that, according to the Bible, ideology that is truly embraced
will ﬁnd expression in behavior.
M oreover, biblical appropriation involves both being and doing. e Bible
recognizes the necessity of the re-formation of the entire person, beginning
with the person’s character, which the Bible typically calls the “heart,”
meaning the “entire inner life of a person.”[87] For this reason, among
others, one cannot in practice absolutely separate appropriation from
interpretation. Profound moral and spiritual formation of persons and
communities should occur as they read the Bible carefully and as they
faithfully interpret it. Immersing oneself in the study of the Bible has the
power to transform one’s feelings and emotions, attitude, and will.[88] A nd
according to the Bible, this transformation of character will be expressed in
behavior.[89] Jesus articulated a principle that is found throughout the
whole of the Bible: “It is what comes out of a person that deﬁles. For it is
from within, from the human heart, that evil intentions come: fornication,
the, murder. . . . A ll these evil things come from within, and they deﬁle a
person” (M ark 7:21–22).[90]
In addition, biblical appropriation involves both the individual and the
corporate body of the church. e Bible is concerned not only with the
thinking and behavior of persons but also with the life of the faith
community in the large. A dmittedly, in one sense community decision is an
abstraction because community decision making is necessarily a product of
the decisions of individuals within the community; but the Bible emphasizes
the ordering of the life of G od’s people with the intention that through its
corporate life, G od’s people might render acceptable worship to G od and
mediate the saving revelation of G od to the world. Hence, both the Old
Testament and the New Testament speak of the community of faith as a
“holy priesthood” (1 Pet. 2:5) or “a priestly kingdom and a holy nation”
(Exod. 19:6; cf. 1 Pet. 2:9); and the New Testament speaks of the corporate
body of the church as the temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Cor. 3:16–17). Indeed,
Paul can say to the Corinthians that they embody Paul’s apostolic

--- Page 355 ---
proclamation to the world: “You yourselves are our letter, . . . to be known
and read by all” (2 Cor. 3:2).[91]
